s1.syndrome_frame: Progressive vertigo with severe headaches and nausea, associated with a cerebellar mass and surrounding edema
salient_findings: Severe bifrontal throbbing headaches with nausea and vomiting
Positive right-sided Dix-Hallpike maneuver with horizontal nystagmus
3 cm left cerebellar hemispheric mass with surrounding vasogenic edema
key_facts: 74-year-old man with a history of metastatic prostate cancer
Known left upper lobe lung mass
Stage III prostate adenocarcinoma treated with prostatectomy and radiation in 2013
Detection of bilateral lung nodules and sclerotic bone lesions in 2016
Biopsy of a left upper lobe lesion confirming mismatch repair deficient, androgen receptor-positive metastatic prostate cancer in 2020
Treated with enzalutamide, then abiraterone acetate and prednisone, and palliative radiation
Presented with four weeks of progressive vertigo
Developed severe bifrontal throbbing headaches with nausea and vomiting a few days before admission
Tested positive for adenovirus at an outside emergency department
Vital signs: temperature 37°C, heart rate 90 beats/min, blood pressure 164/81 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air
Noncontrast head CT showed a 3 cm left cerebellar hemispheric mass with surrounding vasogenic edema
MRI of the brain demonstrated a cystic enhancing lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere with mass effect

shortlist.label: Cerebellar metastasis from prostate cancer
shortlist.why_kept: History of metastatic prostate cancer and presence of a cerebellar mass

shortlist.label: Hemangioblastoma
shortlist.why_kept: Cystic enhancing lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere with mass effect, consistent with hemangioblastoma

shortlist.label: Cerebellar glioblastoma
shortlist.why_kept: Aggressive nature of the cerebellar mass and surrounding edema, consistent with a high-grade glioma

shortlist.label: Cerebellar astrocytoma
shortlist.why_kept: Presence of a cerebellar mass with surrounding edema, and the patient's age, making a glioma a plausible diagnosis

shortlist.label: Cerebellar infarction
shortlist.why_kept: Sudden onset of vertigo and headaches, which could be consistent with a cerebellar stroke

raw.rationale: The patient has a history of metastatic prostate cancer with known lung and bone metastases, and the presence of a cerebellar mass is consistent with metastatic disease, especially given the patient's oncology history and the absence of other explanations for the cerebellar lesion

rejected.label: Hemangioblastoma
rejected.why: While considered, the patient's history of metastatic cancer makes a metastasis more likely

rejected.label: Cerebellar glioblastoma
rejected.why: No evidence of a primary brain tumor in the patient's history

rejected.label: Cerebellar astrocytoma
rejected.why: No evidence of a primary brain tumor in the patient's history

rejected.label: Cerebellar infarction
rejected.why: Imaging findings are more consistent with a mass lesion than an infarct
